title: The depth, length and breadth of an idea: iyun, ma'amik and the bond of daas
overview:
The *Kuntres HaHispaalus* taught that true excitement about G-d must come from a detailed *hisbonenus*. Chapters 1 and 2 explain what *hisbonenus* is by explaining *chachma*, *bina* and *daas*. *Hisbonenus* is *iyun*: dwelling on an idea until it is known in every part, unlike *girsa*, the glance at a passing car.

Why can't you learn it once and get it? Every idea has breadth, length and depth, like a river whose fast inner current is its essence. The depth is never seen directly: it is reached only through the length and breadth, the way a child adding apples finally *chaps* how to add. *Chachma* too has a depth, like a spring fed by a hidden aquifer, and through the depth of *bina*, the fiftieth gate, one reaches it: it is the same water. That is *ma'amik*, and the *navon* who understands one thing from another. What the world calls *ha'amakas hadaas* is not the learning itself. *Daas* is the bond of feeling, the interest that keeps the *iyun* going in the right place; it narrows where *bina* spreads, and the two depend on each other.

sections.title: What hisbonenus is: the inner side of bina, called iyun
sections.summary: True excitement about G-d has to come from a detailed *hisbonenus* (contemplation), so first one must know what it is: gazing hard into the depth of an idea and dwelling on it until it is understood clearly in every part. That is the inner side of *bina*, which the *Gemara* calls *iyun*.

phrases.en: all the particular ways or types of excitement that are born in the mind, heart, and thought from a *hisbonenus*, according to the different levels of the soul, the five levels of the soul, *nefesh*, *ruach*, *neshama*, *chaya*, *yechida*.

blocks.text:
Chapter 1. Chapters 23 and 24 explained the *Keser* (crown) of *Atzilus*. Chapter 25 explains how it is drawn into *Abba* and *Ima*, the *chachma* (wisdom) and *bina* (understanding) of *Atzilus*, but does not explain them there, because chapters 1 and 2 already did.

Those chapters serve a double purpose: they explain *chachma*, *bina* and *daas* (knowledge) as part of the ten *sefiros* (the Divine attributes), and they show how they work in *hisbonenus* (contemplation). So we go back and learn them now.

**It was already explained at length in a special *kuntres*** (tract): the *Kuntres HaHispaalus* (the Tract on Ecstasy). It explains all the types of *hispaalus* (excitement) born in the mind, heart and thought from a *hisbonenus*, according to the five levels of the soul: *nefesh*, *ruach*, *neshama*, *chaya* and *yechida*.

There it explains two levels of *machshava* (thought), cold and hot; then excitement in the heart, in the mind, and of the inner *ratzon* (will): the five levels of the soul, five of the animal soul and five of the G-dly soul.

The main point of that *kuntres*: what level of *hispaalus* you get depends mainly on how refined you are, on the root of your soul, and the level itself does not really matter. What matters is that it be true *avoda* (divine service), and to be true it has to come from a detailed *hisbonenus* in *Elokus* (G-dliness).

**Now**, since excitement about *Elokus*, loving and fearing G-d as opposed to other things, needs *hisbonenus*, **we have to understand what *hisbonenus* is**, so we can do it: **what it is essentially, and what we should contemplate on.** First how to do it, then what to do it on.

That is the subject of the first nine chapters. Chapters 1 and 2 begin by explaining *Chabad* (*chachma*, *bina* and *daas*) in order to explain how to do *hisbonenus*.

blocks.text: The technical definition of *hisbonenus*: **It means to gaze very deeply, very strongly into the depth of an idea**, with your mind's eye. **And you should dwell on it for a long time**: stand over it and watch it, let it take hold in your mind, turn it over and examine it from every angle, **until you understand it clearly, with all of its parts, in minute detail.**

phrases.en: this is the idea of the *pnimiyus* of *bina*,
This is what the *Gemara* calls *iyun*.
like it says in *Gemara*, in *Maseches Sukka*,
One would learn to amass knowledge, one would learn the *girsa*; and the other one would learn in depth.

blocks.text: **This is the idea of the *pnimiyus* of *bina***, the inner side of *bina*. *Bina* means to learn; its *pnimiyus* (inner side) is to learn until you understand a thing clearly in all its parts, as against its external function, understanding something at the surface. **This is what the *Gemara* calls *iyun*** (close analysis).

So now we have the technical definition: *hisbonenus* is *iyun*, examining an idea until you understand it clearly in all its parts. That is the *pnimiyus* of *bina*; *girsa* (knowing the text by rote), learning on the surface, is its *chitzoniyus* (outer side).

**Like it says in *Gemara*, in *Maseches Sukka***, there were two sages: **One would learn to amass knowledge, one would learn the *girsa*; and the other one would learn in depth.**

Both are *bina*: any learning is analyzing, studying, making yourself understand. But understanding only the surface is not the main thing of *bina*. The main thing is to understand into a thing, to know all its little details and parts, not just get a general idea of it.

sections.title: Girsa: understanding at first glance, like a car going by
sections.summary: *Girsa* is understanding at first glance, flowing on without stopping, like noticing a car drive past: soon forgotten, and all one can tell is "I saw a car." A *sevara* glanced at with the mind is the same, and so is a world walked through without stopping to see G-dliness in it.

blocks.text: **The meaning of *girsa*, is just to understand something according to one's first glance.** You look it over once, and whatever idea you get, that's it; **you flow onto the next thing very quickly, without pausing or stopping to dwell on it at all.** *Girsa* is learning to cover ground: you get the basic idea and go on.

blocks.text: A *mashal* (analogy): someone glances at something and doesn't contemplate at all what he is seeing, **how it works and what it is, with all of its parts, its internal parts and its external parts**; **he just glances at it in a passing way.**

blocks.title: A car drives by
blocks.text: You are walking down the street and a car drives by. You know it's a car. But you didn't stop to examine it: a regular car or a hybrid, what kind of engine, how many cylinders? None of the details.

blocks.text: **As time passes, you'll totally forget that it happened**; it wasn't important and you didn't think about it. Even right after, asked what you saw, all you can say is that you saw a car. No details, **because it was just seen with a passing eye**, with no real sinking in: knowing the little details until you are intimate with the thing and recognize it right away.

phrases.he: וכן העברת עין השכל באיזה סברא בהשקפה ראשונה
phrases.en: and the same thing applies to just glancing with your mind at some *sevara* with just the first glance,

phrases.he: בלתי עכוב והעמדה לעיין בו היטב,
phrases.en: without pausing and stopping to examine it well,

phrases.he: ולא ידע בסברא זו לתכליתה כלל
phrases.en: you will not really know the *sevara* in its fullest at all.

blocks.text: The same with **just glancing with your mind at some *sevara*** (a line of reasoning) **without pausing and stopping to examine it well**: you will have a general idea, but **you will not really know the *sevara* in its fullest at all.** To know what the question was, what the answer is, why we are compelled to say this and not something else, what supports it, you have to study *b'iyun* (in depth): ask questions, find answers, ask harder questions, and keep digging until it is really clear.

So with *hisbonenus*. As the Rebbe says, just as you learn *Gemara b'iyun*, you should learn *Chassidus b'iyun*.

And so with the world, G-d's book. We cannot just walk around in life seeing G-dliness without stopping to think, to see what is going on around us, to notice *hashgacha pratis* (Divine providence). That is one of the main ideas of *avoda*: *hisbonenus* not only in the book but in the world; the books help you do it properly.

To explain the difference between *iyun* and *girsa*, he will explain that every idea has three dimensions: length, width and depth. This answers an unasked question: why must we learn *b'iyun*, spend time, ask, examine every detail? Say we're smart and quick; it says in places that the first glance can never grasp the depth of an idea. Why not?

And the same with the world: why can't a person just walk down the street and see G-dliness? Why does he have to work, do *avoda* and do this *hisbonenus*, before *davenen* (praying) and during it?

sections.title: Every idea has breadth, length and depth, like a river
sections.summary: Breadth is explaining an idea to every side in many details; length is bringing it down into *meshalim* until a small child can grasp it; depth is its essential point, like the fast inner current of a river from which all the rest of the water spreads. Everything comes from the depth, and the depth is reached only through the length and the breadth.

phrases.he: כי הנה ג' דברים הוא שיש בכל דבר מושכל.
phrases.en: There are three things or three aspects to every idea:
There is the depth of the idea, the length of the idea, and the width of the idea.

blocks.text: For **there are three things or three aspects to every idea**: *omek*, *orech* and *rochav*. **There is the depth of the idea, the length of the idea, and the width of the idea.** Now he explains these three dimensions.

blocks.text: **The width of an idea means to explain the idea to every side with a lot of details, like the width of a river**, **and not just saying things like they are in the shortest way, which would be like a narrow river.** The analogy carries over into English: a broad idea is one with many parts, many fields and subjects within it.

blocks.title: Medicine, a broad subject
blocks.text:
Medicine is a broad idea: so many fields and types of doctors, specialists in every part of the body, and all these theories, Western, Eastern, holistic, and not everybody agrees which of them belong to medicine and which are just quackery.

In the narrowest way you would say medicine is "the science of healing the body," a dictionary definition: a narrow river. Explaining all its aspects broadens it.

phrases.he: עד להביאו בהשגות התינוק קטן כו',

blocks.text: **The length of the idea is a measure of the intensity of the descent of the idea to enclothe it into *meshalim*** (analogies), **until you bring the idea to within the grasp of even a small child**: how hard it is to explain simply. A very deep idea takes a very talented teacher to put into simple *meshalim* a small child can understand.

An idea that is not so deep is easy to explain to a child; it is child-like anyway. Football is not so deep. Simpler still is tiddlywinks, which a really little kid can play: a short cup, flat round discs like coins, and you flip the discs into the cup. That is the whole game, pretty short, and very narrow too.

blocks.title: One apple plus one apple
blocks.text:
You see these dimensions teaching a little kid addition. The whole width, all the problems and examples, is too much. Even one idea, one plus one is two, is too abstract. So you put it in a *mashal*: one apple plus one apple is two apples, "one fishy plus one fishy is two fishies," and the kid starts to understand.

That is the length: from one plus one, the abstract, down to apples. Not such a far descent; a deeper idea has farther to go.

The length is potential and actual. The potential length depends on the idea: the deeper, the longer (as he will say, width and length depend on depth). The actual length depends on how far apart teacher and student are. A teacher of very deep understanding is like a mountain, a shallow student like a little valley, and the idea has to flow a long way from one to the other.
**Like a river that flows and is drawn out for a long time, a long way**: like a river flowing from a mountain. From a high mountain down to a low place, that is very, very long.

**As explained at length in the *Kesavim***: as *HaYom Yom* says, the name for the longest *maamarim* (discourses) the Alter Rebbe said at the end of his life, his manuscripts. They explain it **about the length of the skins that covered the *Mishkan***.

There it explains length from the verses: the skins are to be thirty *amos* long "by the *ama*." Why repeat *ama*? Because length is the same thing doubled over: you take an *ama* of skin, then another and another, attach them, fold them over, and it becomes long.

That is a *mashal* for an idea going from teacher to student to student. It is the same idea, but it passes through many minds, each explaining it a little differently, so it went a long way. Or within one teacher: from one explanation to a simpler one and a simpler one, applied at lower and lower levels until it is very simple. That too is length.

blocks.title: The continental divide
blocks.text: A river starts from a spring in the mountains, or a spring with melting snow and rainwater collected from different mountains. In America the Rocky Mountains run from Mexico up to Canada and split the country, not in half, since they are far to the west: the continental divide. Rain falling west of it joins little streams, then bigger ones, then rivers, and flows to the Pacific. Of all the rain, some soaks in and grows crops, some evaporates, and the rest becomes rivers. And then there are springs.

The flowing water carves a groove in the ground. At the bottom and sides it drags against the ground, on top against the air; that makes a cushion, and in the middle, "like a lubricated tube," a stream flows very fast. That is the main flow of the river, the undercurrent; the water on the sides and top is much slower. When the difference is big it is dangerous for swimming: it can pull someone under.

That flow is the main thing in a river: it is trying to get from the mountains to the ocean. Where the land flattens it spills over and becomes wide, and it can go a long way. With too little water it flows a bit, soaks into the ground and dries up; it takes a lot of water to reach the ocean.

blocks.title: When the child chaps how to add
blocks.text:
Teaching children to add, you first bring it down to physical examples: one apple plus one apple, one fishy plus one fishy. After a few *meshalim* they understand that one problem; that is the length. Then two apples plus two apples, and more, until they see the common denominator, the central point of adding.

At a certain point they *chap* it (Yiddish: catch it). Now they need no more examples. Apples, fish, chairs or books, one plus two or two plus two, any number: they just know how to add. That is the point, the depth.

blocks.text: Once you have that, you can bring it into any length automatically. Ask the child to add apples and of course he can; what's the difference? To the essential point, abstract or concrete is the same. And two seven-digit numbers are not harder, just adding over and over with the rules of carrying; it only takes more work. All the particular problems you can do: that is the width, and it comes from having the depth.

So why not just teach the kids the depth? This is the main point: the depth cannot be grasped without the length and the width. You never see the depth directly, only as it is expressed in them.

The more you have the depth, the more length and width you can bring out; and the more you study the length and width, the more you grasp the depth. That's the rule, and that is why understanding needs *iyun*: studying the length and the width to grasp the depth.

Back to the parenthesis about the height: from the idea you go up and up, **until you reach the depth of above**, the highest height, **like in the time of the flood of Noach, that the water went higher and higher until it covered everything.**

**And the same thing will happen spiritually in the time of *Moshiach***, **in the 500th year of the life of Noach**. Noach is called a *tzaddik* (righteous man), so he stands for *yesod*, which corresponds to the sixth millennium, the one we are in, from 5000 to 6000; his five hundredth year is 5500. So from halfway through the sixth millennium a spiritual flood began, preparing the world for *Moshiach*, the seventh millennium.

**As it says in the *Zohar* about that time**, **all the gateways of *chachma* opened up**, secular and G-dly knowledge alike. There was a big boost in science, and *pnimiyus haTorah* (the inner Torah) and *Chassidus* began to spread.

**And this is the wellsprings of the depth of the *chachma* that got stronger, they went higher and higher, and they covered all the mountains**: the geysers bursting from the bottom of the earth. **And the reservoirs of the heavens opened up also**, bringing down the water above the heavens, the depth of above, **which depends on the depth below, because the beginning is wedged in the end.**

This is explained in two ways. In one, the depth below, the wellsprings, is secular knowledge, the knowledge of this world; as the sciences advance more and more, they help open up the knowledge of G-dliness too, so that we will see G-dliness in the world.

The other, Reb Hillel of Paritch's in his commentary, more in line with the book: doing *iyun* is opening the wellsprings of *chachma*, digging into the earth to bring out the hidden water, delving into an idea to uncover its hidden depth. That automatically opens a person's *chachma*, which is higher than the world, and he gets a *chiddush* (a new insight), a flash. But to get it he must do the *iyun*, because the end is wedged in the beginning: studying the idea over and over reaches its essence, which is higher even than *chachma*, and so opens the *chachma* itself.

As the verse says, **Either cast your question to the depth, means to go deep, or to raise it up on high.** In a way deep and high are synonymous; but first you go to the depth, and afterwards you raise it up to the height. First the *bina*, the *hisbonenus*; then you get the *chachma*. So **it explains in the *Kesavim*, in the long *maamar* of the Alter Rebbe.**

Back to the point: length, width and height, **it all comes from the essential depth, which is the point of the idea, the way that it flows out from the *chachma***. *Chachma* is called *ayin* (nothing): an abstract point, a nothing beside *bina*'s concrete, tangible explanation. **Like it says, that the river went out from *Eden***: **because *bina* is called a river**, flowing from its source, **and *chachma* is called the wellspring, the source itself, as is known.**

sections.title: Iyun: dwelling on the idea, a vessel for the depth of bina
sections.summary: *Iyun* is to stand over an idea and study it very much, the opposite of rushing, until one knows it inside and out, which is why *hisbonenus* has a double *nun*. *Iyun* is only a vessel for the depth of *bina*; what the world calls *ha'amakas hadaas*, concentration, is not *iyun*, and it helps only after the idea has been studied.

blocks.title: The craftsman takes it apart
blocks.text: You bring a broken thing to a craftsman and ask what's broken. He turns it over carefully, takes it all apart and examines every piece: does it need cleaning, fixing or replacing? He lays it all out on the table, sees what's what, and knows all of its details.

blocks.text:
**And this is what is called *hisbonenus*, with a double *nun*.** It comes from *bina*, making yourself understand, and should have one *nun*: *hisbinus*. The double *nun* is an intense form of the verb: *hisbinus* would be *girsa*, *hisbonenus* is *iyun*. It also hints that you go over the idea again and again; you can't learn it just once.

So the double *nun*, **because that implies that you're *misbonen*** (contemplating) **and you're studying it a lot**, as **Rashi explains, *b'iyuni***: **to dwell on an idea until you understand it clearly with all its parts.**

phrases.en: comes out,

phrases.he: בחינת העיון הזה הוא רק בחינת כלי לבחינת ההעמקה דבינה עצמה,
phrases.en: that this thing of *iyun*, of analyzing the subject, is only like a vessel, it's only a tool for the actual delving of *bina* itself.

phrases.he: כי לכאורה בחינת העיון הזה נקרא העמקת הדעת בלשון בעולם,
phrases.en: Seemingly, what we just described as *iyun* is what the world calls *ha'amakas hadaas*.
but this is not true, this is not so.

phrases.he: דהעמקת הדעת היינו בחינת כלי לבד
phrases.en: that *ha'amakas hadaas* is also only a *kli*, it's also only a tool,
to come to the true depth of the idea

blocks.text: It **comes out** that *iyun* is only a vessel for *bina*'s delving. Everything comes from the depth, so the more of it you grasp, the more length and width you have, the more ways you can apply it and explain it simply. But a student starting out can reach the depth only through the length and the width. They are a shell around it, and you have to crack it; the more of the whole length and width you go through, the more you find the depth behind it.

So **this thing of *iyun*, of analyzing the subject, is only like a vessel, it's only a tool for the actual delving of *bina* itself.** *Iyun* is just dwelling on the idea a long time instead of passing over it. An idea that passes quickly gives your *bina* no chance to focus on it and "do its magic." Held in the mind a long time, it lets *bina* analyze it, become sensitive to it and find the depth.

Going further: **Seemingly, what we just described as *iyun* is what the world calls *ha'amakas hadaas*** (deep concentration): meditation, holding an idea in mind a long time so that the focus by itself brings a flash from *chachma*. **But this is not true, this is not so.** It is not *iyun* or *hisbonenus*. *Ha'amakas hadaas* **is also only a *kli***, a tool, but a tool **to come to the true depth of the idea**, higher even than what *bina* gives you.

The rest of the chapter explains *chachma*, which also has a length, width and depth that one can go deeper into, and then *daas*, and how *bina* and *daas* each give something and have to work together. But the basic idea is this: concentration, focusing your mind on an idea, does not make you understand it. Studying the explanations makes you understand it.

Just meditating on an idea, focusing on it to attune yourself and cultivate a sensitivity to it, "will not do anything, at least nothing positive." Later he will say what negative things can happen from that kind of meditation without first studying, without the *bina*.

But when you study, obviously, if you don't concentrate and put yourself into it, you won't understand. As the famous *HaYom Yom* says, the main thing in understanding *Chassidus* is to feel that it is *noge'a* (relevant) to you, that it relates to yourself.

blocks.title: Rabbi Meir and the woman's chicken
blocks.text: A story in the *Gemara*, brought in *HaYom Yom*: in the *beis midrash* they were discussing whether a chicken was kosher, and Rabbi Meir kept bringing ingenious arguments, the craziest things, that it was. They kept telling him to give it up: the chicken is not kosher. Then he said, "I promise you that all of these arguments were told to me by a woman that brought me a chicken."

She was not learned or necessarily smart, but she really wanted that chicken to be kosher, so she thought up all these arguments. So too, someone not so smart or knowledgeable who has a *daas* for a thing, who feels it connects to himself, will really understand it.

Nevertheless, everything that belongs to *daas*, concentrating, meditating, focusing, connecting yourself to the idea, helps only after you have the *bina*: after you have studied the idea and understood it.

blocks.title: Medical school and internship
blocks.text: This holds in any discipline. A medical student has to study all the explanations, the whole length and width, or he will never have the *daas* to be a doctor. Staring at a picture of the anatomy, or any meditation like that, will not make him understand. It takes years of study, then internship: he has to find a doctor who will let him hang around, be his *mashpia* (mentor), and show him how it is actually done.
That is the idea of a *mashpia*. A *mashpia* is many things, but one of the main ones is that he is your guide and mentor in *avodas Hashem* (the service of G-d).

More on *ha'amakas hadaas* and *daas* at the end of the chapter. For now: *bina* gives only the depth of a *musag*, the idea as it is in *bina*. *Daas* connects you to the *chachma* above *bina*, but only after you have the *bina*.

sections.title: Ma'amik: through bina to the depth of chachma, like water traced to its spring
sections.summary: Higher still is *ma'amik*, reaching above *chachma* to its source. *Chachma* too has depth, length and breadth, like a spring fed from a hidden aquifer. The depth of *bina*, the fiftieth gate, seems no match for the depth of *chachma*; but it is the same water, so whoever delves into the *musag* taps its source and draws new *chiddushim* of *chachma* into *bina*.

blocks.text: So whatever you want, the depth of *bina*, *chachma*, its depth, all the way to the depth of *Keser*, the *etzem* (essence): how do you get it? Take the *sefer*, the *maamar*, and learn it. Then learn it again, and again, not just more times but more in depth. Ask questions and answer them; learn it with someone for a fresh perspective. Imagine giving a class on it to "totally skeptical intellectual people": what will they ask, how will I explain it? Think what the *nimshal* (what the analogy stands for) is, how to apply it, what the examples are, until you really understand it.

blocks.text: Just keep working on the idea itself, the same words and ideas, and that *iyun*, that *hisbonenus*, will automatically bring you deeper: first the depth of *bina*, then the *chachma*, eventually its source. So you have something to work with: a *yesh*, the explanations of *bina*, and the *bina* will open up the *chachma* and even the *Keser*. And, as the next chapter says, everything under it too: the *middos* (emotions) and the *maaseh* (action).

This is the whole *shita* (approach) of *Chabad*: *hisbonenus* changes your perspective, changes your feelings and brings you to action. This chapter and the next give the philosophical grounds for the *Chabad* approach to self-improvement, to *avoda* on yourself. *Hisbonenus* will bring you all the way to the source of *chachma*.

**This is called the depths of *chachma*, or the hidden *chachma***, *taalumos chachma*. **For just like there's a length, width, and depth in *bina*, which like we said before is called a *yesh***: something tangible you can explain and work with, a particular explanation. Rashi explains the *Gemara* to you, and his explanation is a very concrete thing, a *yesh*; Tosafos explains it another way, and that is a *yesh* too.

Or the kid told that one apple and one apple are two apples; even one plus one is two is a concrete example, a particular problem. The concept of math behind it is an abstract point, much harder to talk about. **So too there's a length, width, and depth to the wellspring of *chachma*, which is called a nothing**, an abstract point.

blocks.text: Now the dimensions of *chachma*. Just as in *bina* you go through the length and width to get the depth, and there is always more to do, so within *chachma* a person can perceive its point more and more deeply.

blocks.title: The underground lake and the mountain spring water
blocks.text:
**What's the depth of the wellspring? The depth of the wellspring is its original root, where it's cut out in the stone deep in the ground**: an underground lake, with a crack wiggling up through the earth's crust until the water spurts out, the *maayan* (wellspring). "And then they bottle it, and they sell it to you as mountain spring water."

**And from there, its flow spreads up until it bursts through the earth, and it comes out drop by drop, and now it's coming revealed from its hidden source.** Underground you see no water; you have to dig. Wherever you are, he thinks, if you dig deep enough you'll hit the water table.

**And the deeper you go, the more hidden it is**: **like it says by the *Mabul*** (the Flood) **that the *maayanos* of the abyss, the very deep underground lakes, burst forth.** Some springs and geysers are normally open; others are too deep even for a well. In the *Mabul* they all burst, and it rained too. **For the earth is riddled with veins**, of water, gold, silver, and the veins of water have a first source: in English, the aquifer. There are underground lakes, rivers between them, and cracks that bring the water up; that is where wellsprings come from.

That is the *mashal*. **And this is what it says, that *chachma* is found from nothing**: **that it comes out from the concealed source of *chachma*, which is called the depth of *chachma*.** The hidden underground lake is the depth, the *omek*. The width is how wide the crack is, all the way up to where you see a wellspring. The length is the spring dripping out and flowing down to the river. Now to explain what *chachma* is.

phrases.he: והחכמה הוא המצאת שכל החדש שיוצא כברק כו'
phrases.en: The power of *chachma* is the ability to find a new idea that comes out like a lightning bolt, like a flash,
as known,

phrases.en: the source where it comes from under the ground is the main, the main real self, the main *etzem* of the *chachma*, and that's its real inwardness

blocks.text: **The power of *chachma* is the ability to find a new idea that comes out like a lightning bolt, like a flash**: you think and think and, boom, you get an idea. Like a wellspring: water you saw nowhere, hidden under the ground, suddenly pops out. So *chachma* brings a new idea out of its source.

As with *bina*, whose depth is the main thing and the source of its length and width, **the source where it comes from under the ground**, the big lake, **is the main, the main real self, the main *etzem* of the *chachma*, and that's its real inwardness.** Behind the *chachma* is a hidden potential, the *koach hamaskil* (the power of insight): a hidden reservoir of knowledge and ability to understand, coming out in different ways in the *chachma*.

blocks.text: **Like we're saying before about the depth of the concept in *bina***, that is not the deepest depth. **That's only the depth of the idea the way that it's understood in *bina*, and it's felt as like a concrete thing, as like a *yesh***: **I understood something with a revealed *sevara***, one I can explain logically in words. The point of *chachma* is beyond that, something you have to *chap*, much harder to articulate. **Because the depth of this explanation of the idea is only the *ayin* of the *yesh***: the abstract point behind these explanations, but still their point.

blocks.title: One Rashi, and the point in every Rashi
blocks.text:
You learn a Rashi on the *Gemara*. At first you don't get it; you review it until you understand his *chiddush*, his question and his answer. Or you go to a Rashi *sicha* (talk of the Rebbe on Rashi), which really goes a little past that; but say you just learned the Rashi and really got it. That is the depth of the *bina*: you understand the explanation here.

Go deeper and you start to get a *chachma*: you see that this Rashi represents a *shita* (system), a point you find in every Rashi, or at least in many.

That already brings out a *chachma*, a much more abstract depth. Then you see a *machlokes* (dispute) between Rashi and Tosafos running through many arguments, until you find the source of how he explains every *Gemara*. A *sicha* sometimes brings this out, as the Rogatchover sometimes does. To see it you must learn many Rashis, all *b'iyun*, "or if you learn a Rashi sicha, then you can cheat."

So the first Rashi did give you an abstract depth, its point, which you cannot explain, only get. Still, it is not the real depth, **and it's not comparable to the abstract point of *chachma* before it comes into the whole world of understanding.**

blocks.title: Koach and poel
blocks.text: The abstract point of *chachma* comes before it is applied to any instance. The Rebbe explains the *machlokes* between Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel as *koach* (potential) and *poel* (actual), which explains many disputes. *Koach* and *poel* is a *chachma*, related to nothing in particular; at a given dispute you ask how it looks from the side of *koach* and how from the side of *poel*. So **not even the depth of the explanation of *bina***, its distilled essence, compares to the *ayin* of *chachma*.

blocks.question: So how can hisbonenus, which gets only the depth of bina, ever get to chachma?
blocks.text: Seemingly *bina* just does not reach that far. It reaches the depth of *bina*, but it will not get anywhere near even the outside of *chachma*, let alone its depth.

phrases.en: however,

phrases.he: עומק המושג נקרא שער הנו''ן דבינה,
phrases.en: the depth of understanding, which is called the *shaar hanun* of *bina*,
even though it goes from the abstract point of *chachma* to be a *yesh*,
a wellspring is gonna go out from the *Kodesh HaKodashim*.
It's gonna start out very thin and narrow, like the horns of a grasshopper,

phrases.he: שרשו מגיע בעומק דחכמה הנזכר לעיל,
phrases.en: its source reaches all the way up to the depth of *chachma* that he mentioned before.
and like we see tangibly,
that anybody that just studies and goes deeper into the depth of the *musag*, of the explanation of whatever he's learning,
he taps into the source and the root of the concept the way it's all the way in *chachma*,

phrases.he: להמציא בחינת חדשות דאור החכמה בבינה,
phrases.en: to bring in new *chiddushim*, to bring in new ideas from the light of *chachma* into *bina*.
and this is what's called *ma'amik*, that it causes to deepen.
that it activates,
because it activates the depth of *chachma* and *bina* and causes them to come out and open up.

blocks.text: **However**, it is not so: through the *iyun* of *bina* you reach the depth of *chachma*, up to the inner *Keser*. For **the depth of understanding, which is called the *shaar hanun* of *bina*** (the fiftieth gate), **even though it goes from the abstract point of *chachma* to be a *yesh***, seen only as applied in this example: **its source reaches all the way up to the depth of *chachma* that he mentioned before.** It may be only one example, but it is the depth itself, the actual point, with the whole *etzem* in it; at the *shaar hanun* it opens all the way to *chachma* and the *Keser*.

The *shaar hanun* will be explained later, but basically: in *Sefiras HaOmer* (the counting of the Omer) we count *chesed*, *chesed* of *chesed* and so on, the *middos* of *bina*. The fiftieth day, *Shavuos*, is the depth of *bina* itself, the *Keser*, *chachma* and *bina* of *bina*, source of the *middos*: the *etzem* of the idea, higher than explaining or applying. So we don't count it; it comes from above once you do your work. Your work is the *middos*: in *halacha* (Jewish law), the laws of what is kosher and what is unfit. Know them clearly and you will have the *mochin* (intellectual faculties) of why yes and why no, the depth, up to the real *etzem*.

Now the parentheses. When *Moshiach* comes, **a wellspring is gonna go out from the *Kodesh HaKodashim*** (the Holy of Holies). **It's gonna start out very thin and narrow, like the horns of a grasshopper**, then like a string, a thicker string, until it is as wide as a rushing river. The *Kodesh HaKodashim* is the *Keser*, the source, where the *etzem* is revealed; the wellspring is *chachma*, the river *bina*. Both come from the same place. *Chachma* stays at the source and the river goes out, but it is the same water.

So though the depth of *bina* leaves the source and is applied only in a particular example, the *etzem* is *mamash* there, as it is in this example. Understand it here and you understand it in every example; you only have to learn to uncover what is external, what can change, what is just a garment, and what is the real *etzem*. Find that, and it is the same for everything else.

blocks.title: The same water, traced back to the aquifer
blocks.text: So **its source reaches all the way up to the depth of *chachma***. Trace a river up and it comes from the wellspring; keep tracing its water down the wellspring, through the veins in the earth's crust, to the aquifer. It is the same water; it just came all the way down the mountain to you. So any little concrete explanation in *bina*, an example, holds the entire *chachma* hidden in it, down to its depth, because you have a little of the essence. "It's the same water," however far from the source it came out.

blocks.title: One taste of the chocolate bar
blocks.text: Taste one little example of a chocolate bar and you may not know all its forms or uses, but you have the essence: you know what it is and how it tastes, because that stays the same. The external things change; the inner point, the *shaar hanun*, stays the same in *chachma* and in the *Keser*.

On the contrary, in *bina*, where it is very tangible, is where you can really get it. *Chachma* is far beyond *bina*, abstract where *bina* is concrete, yet the depth of *bina* reaches past *chachma* to the *Keser*, its source. That is what we set out to explain: through *iyun*, learning explanations, you can get new *chachmos*, a *chiddush* in *chachma*, activating the depth of *chachma*.

**And like we see tangibly, that anybody that just studies and goes deeper into the depth of the *musag*** (the concept as grasped), **of the explanation of whatever he's learning**, taps into the root of the concept in *chachma*, **to bring in new *chiddushim*, to bring in new ideas from the light of *chachma* into *bina***. **And this is what's called *ma'amik*, that it causes to deepen**, a causative form: **it activates the depth of *chachma* and *bina* and causes them to come out and open up.** But indirectly. You cannot just walk into the *Kodesh HaKodashim*, which is why that was the *mashal*; but working to understand the *bina* better automatically brings out more and more of the *chachma*, up to the *Keser*.

blocks.title: Kuntres Etz HaChaim: how to learn Gemara
blocks.text:
The Rebbe Rashab explains all this for learning *Gemara* in *Kuntres Etz HaChaim*, chapters 26 to 30, telling the *bochurim* (students) of *Tomchei Temimim* how to learn: the same process chapters 1 and 2 here give for *Chassidus* and contemplating G-dliness.

Don't try to make *chiddushim*, novel approaches, a whole *pilpul* (Talmudic debate). Just understand very clearly what the *Gemara* says: the *bina*, the *hisbonenus*. The more clearly you do, the more *chiddushim* come by themselves. Once the basic *pshat* (plain meaning) is clear, if you have a good mind for it, go deeper with *diyukim* (precise inferences) in the exact wording and order of the *Mishna*, and get deeper *chiddushim*.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 14 finishes line 28 (w0-139) and goes on explaining it; line 29 is read only in class 15.

blocks.text: The basic *pshat* is like *bina*; the *diyukim* are like *ma'amik*. In both, your focus is only to understand what the *Gemara* says. Be very careful not to be making a *chiddush*, and that everything is true: a *pshat* or *diyuk* must be compelling, definitely true to what it says there. Then you will understand very well, and the *chiddushim* come automatically.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 14 finishes line 28 (w0-139) and goes on explaining it; line 29 is read only in class 15.

blocks.text:
The same with anything: research in medicine, cars, space ships, computers. To succeed, scientists have to study what is known and understand very well how it works; then they can tap into the *chachma* behind it and innovate.

But sometimes, especially in medicine, people working for grants, or writing a PhD thesis, have to come up with a *chiddush*, a new discovery, and that can lead to dishonesty: they are trying to invent something more than to understand what is true. That is not the way to do it. Understand everything very clearly, and all this will come by itself.

blocks.title: The fiftieth gate in one plus one
blocks.text: Even the simplest explanation of something holds the depth of the whole wisdom, up to its source, where it connects to other wisdom. When a little kid understands one apple plus one apple is two apples, he gets the entire *shaar hanun*, the fiftieth gate of *bina*, in a very small way; and that point includes the whole *chachma* of mathematics, even where it connects to music and art.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 14 finishes line 28 (w0-139) and goes on explaining it; line 29 is read only in class 15.

blocks.title: One plus one is one: mathematics as a language
blocks.text: The depth in one plus one is two is seeing two separate things as forming a unit. One apple and another apple are separate and stay separate, but instead of this apple and that apple you call them two apples. Something outside them connects them, though they stay separate.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 14 finishes line 28 (w0-139) and goes on explaining it; line 29 is read only in class 15.

blocks.text: That is the basis of our mathematics, because at essence mathematics is a language, a way of describing the world, and you could describe it otherwise. Stick two pieces of clay into one big piece: one plus one is one. Or see no common denominator between this apple and that apple: "So, 1 1 1 1"; they are separate, so why view them as one thing? Our mathematics is a level of relationship where things are separate yet something higher connects them.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 14 finishes line 28 (w0-139) and goes on explaining it; line 29 is read only in class 15.

blocks.text:
Traced to its source, this is *Echad*, of chapters 10 and 11: *Yachid*, *Echad* and *Kadmon*. At *Yachid* everything is completely one, and one plus one would be one. At *Echad* things are separate and stay separate, yet something connects them: everything in the world reveals the one G-d. At *Kadmon* everything is separate and unique, and you cannot really count.

That is why you are not supposed to count people: as a number you lose sight of their individuality. Have them by name, not by number, because each person is a completely different world and you can't lump them together.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 14 finishes line 28 (w0-139) and goes on explaining it; line 29 is read only in class 15.

blocks.title: Separate notes, one melody
blocks.text: That perspective of *Echad* also gives us music. Its depth is that we hear completely separate notes as one flowing thing, a theme, a melody. That is in our minds. If the mind heard each note separately without connecting them, we would hear a bunch of notes, not a song. We hear music because the mind hears the notes' differences and at the same time puts them together into the whole.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 14 finishes line 28 (w0-139) and goes on explaining it; line 29 is read only in class 15.

blocks.title: Brush strokes and pixels, one picture
blocks.text: The same with art. A painting is separate brush strokes, or pixels; the mind sees the contrast of the colors but also puts them together into a picture. Some people, he thinks, born with certain vision problems, even corrected later in life, lack the skill to put things together into a picture as we see it, or to have depth perception. Turning images into what we see takes a lot of interpreting: recognizing the distinctions and at the same time grouping them into a whole.

sections.title: Be wise with understanding, understand with wisdom: the navon who reaches the Keser
sections.summary: *Chacham b'vina* (*Ayin Beis* of *SaG*) is a *chiddush* within the idea one studies, born of the *iyun* that is *bina sheb'bina*; the *Keser* of *bina* is the depth of the concept, rooted in the depth of *chachma*. *Havein b'chachma* (*SaG* of *Ayin Beis*) is the power of explanation within *chachma* itself: the *navon*, whom Moshe could not find, understands one thing from another because he reaches the *Keser* that joins *chachma* and *bina*.

phrases.en: based on this,
this that it says in *Sefer Yetzira*, that you should understand with wisdom and be wise with understanding,

blocks.text: **Based on this**, a parenthesis on how *chachma* and *bina* connect, at their source, with the *Keser*. Simply, *chachma* of *bina* is lower than *bina* of *chachma*: you go up from *bina* of *bina* to *chachma* of *bina*, *Keser* of *bina*, then *bina*, *chachma* and *Keser* of *chachma*. But really, to have *bina* in *chachma* or *chachma* in *bina*, even *chachma* of *bina*, the lowest combination, you must reach the *Keser* above them both that joins them. So even a *chiddush* in *bina* activates the *Keser*, the source of *chachma*.

That is why doing *iyun* in *bina* and getting *chiddushim* there starts to activate real *chiddushim* in *chachma*: in a way, the ability to make a *chiddush* in *bina* is higher than the *chachma* itself. That is what he said before the parenthesis, that *iyun* into the *bina* activates the depth of *chachma* and *bina*, and is called *ma'amik*.

**This that it says in *Sefer Yetzira*** (the Book of Formation), **that you should understand with wisdom and be wise with understanding.** *Havein b'chachma*: from a *chiddush*, a new idea, understand other things. *Vachacham b'vina*: within *bina* have *chachma*, use your understanding to make a *chiddush*.

phrases.en: it's explained in the *maamarim* of the Alter Rebbe that are called *Kesavim*,
*Ayin Beis* of *SaG* means *chachma* within *bina*, and that's *chacham b'vina*, be wise with understanding.

phrases.he: שהוא רק להבין דבר חידוש אחר מתוך המושג דבינה,

phrases.he: שזה אינו אלא על ידי בחינת העיון הנזכר לעיל,
phrases.en: The only way that you'll understand an idea clearly and be able to make a *chiddush*, a new way to explain it or a new way to understand it, is if you study it very very well, which is the idea of *iyun*,

phrases.he: שהוא המברר כל חלקיו על בוריו,
phrases.en: this *iyun* is what clarifies all of the parts, all the details of the idea.
this is what's called *bina sheb'bina*.

blocks.text: **It's explained in the *maamarim* of the Alter Rebbe that are called *Kesavim***: this is *Ayin Beis* of *SaG*, the Names of seventy-two and sixty-three, different spellings of the Name *Havaya*. Spelling out each letter is a *milui* (the spelling out of a letter's name): instead of *yud*, you write *yud-vav-dalet*. All four of these Names will be explained later.

In short, one spelling, corresponding to *chachma*, has a *gematria* (numerical value) of seventy-two, and another, corresponding to *bina*, of sixty-three. So *Ayin Beis* of *SaG* is *chachma* within *bina*, **and that's *chacham b'vina*, be wise with understanding.** *Ayin Beis* is spelled all with *yuds*: *yud-vav-dalet, hei-yud, vav-yud-vav, hei-yud*. *SaG* puts one *alef* in place of a *yud*, nine less: *yud-vav-dalet, hei-yud, vav-alef-vav, hei-yud*.

*Chacham b'vina* is **to make a *chiddush* just within this understanding of *bina***: in the Rashi you are learning, you have a question, and you find a *chiddush* in how to explain it. **The only way that you'll understand an idea clearly and be able to make a *chiddush*** is to study it very well, *iyun*. **This *iyun* is what clarifies all of the parts, all the details of the idea**, and **this is what's called *bina sheb'bina*** (*bina* within *bina*). Through it you come to *chachma sheb'bina*, a *chiddush* within that idea.

phrases.he: ואחר כך יוכל להוליד ולהתחכם להמציא הבנה והשגה חדשה,
phrases.en: and then afterwards you'll be able to bear out a new thing and find a new understanding,

that's called *chachma* of *bina*.

blocks.text: **And then afterwards you'll be able to bear out a new thing and find a new understanding, but only within this idea that you're learning**: not a new idea unrelated to it, just a new way of explaining this. **That's called *chachma* of *bina***: *chachma* means a *chiddush*, *bina* that it is within the understanding.

**But the *Keser* of *bina*, that's the depth of the understanding**, and **its source reaches all the way up to the depth of *chachma* that we mentioned before.** So reaching the *omek hamusag* reaches the source of *chachma* too.

phrases.en: and then understand with wisdom, that's *bina* of *chachma*,
that's the name of 63 within the name of 72, or *bina* within *chachma*,

blocks.text: **And then understand with wisdom, that's *bina* of *chachma***, *SaG* of *Ayin Beis*: **that's the power of explanation that's within *chachma* itself, that you're able to explain the *chachma* in many ways.** You get a new idea, you see its point, and you see how from it you could explain it many ways and apply it to many things.

blocks.title: Seeing the whole thing before describing it
blocks.text: **But this is still higher than an actual understanding in *bina*.** You see the *etzem*, the whole picture, and could explain it in many ways, but you have not brought out an explanation yet. Like seeing something: you see the whole thing and all its details, and if I asked you could keep describing it every way. But right now you have not explained it, not even to yourself.

phrases.en: and this that it says,
he didn't find *nevonim*, he didn't find people of this type of understanding.

phrases.he: שהוא המבין דבר מתוך דבר דוקא
phrases.en: a *navon* is somebody that can understand one thing from something else.

blocks.title: Moshe could not find nevonim
blocks.text: **And this that it says**, *nevonim lo ishtakchu*: Yisro told Moshe Rabbeinu to find judges who were *nevonim*, people of superior understanding. Moshe found people with a lot of the qualifications (Yisro gave him, he thinks, seven), but **he didn't find *nevonim***. There are a lot of very wise, talented people; what is such a big deal about a *navon*?

**A *navon* is somebody that can understand one thing from something else.** What's so hard? It sounds like a logical deduction. It is not just that: it is understanding one thing until you find its point and source, and seeing how that point explains something seemingly completely different and unrelated.

As the Arizal says, someone who knows how to make a *yichud* (union) can know whatever he wants to know: trace an idea up to its source in the *Keser* and bring it down into any *chachma* you want, and from there into any *bina*. That is the *navon*: at will he goes from *bina* to *chachma* and back to any other *bina*, finding the abstract point that unites everything and applying it to anything practical. To move freely like that you must be a master of both, which means reaching the *Keser* that connects them.

phrases.he: היינו מצד שרש כח זה דהבן בחכמה שמגיע בעומק דחכמה הנזכר לעיל,
phrases.en: the ability to do this comes from the *omek* of *chachma*, from the depth of *chachma*, which is the *Keser*.

phrases.he: על כן יוכל להבין דבר חכמה אחרת לגמרי מתוך דבר חכמה זאת
phrases.en: And therefore you're able to take one idea, one *chachma*, and understand from it a completely different idea, a completely different subject.

blocks.text: It is special because **the ability to do this comes from the *omek* of *chachma*, from the depth of *chachma*, which is the *Keser*. And therefore you're able to take one idea, one *chachma*, and understand from it a completely different idea, a completely different subject**: math from music or music from math, math applied to law, law to psychology or physics; or one *sugya* (topic) in *Gittin* applied to *Nezikin*, though they seem totally unrelated.

phrases.en: which this is much higher than a *chacham*,

phrases.en: from just the ability to get a *chiddush*, to understand some new idea,

phrases.he: שאינו מבין ממנה חכמה ושכל אחר

blocks.text: **Which this is much higher than a *chacham*, from just the ability to get a *chiddush***, which **doesn't understand from it a different *sechel*** (intellect). A regular *chacham* (wise man) gets a flash, so good, he gets it. "But he's stuck." If no *chiddush* came in something else, that's it. A *navon* can take whatever he understands and from it understand anything else he wants.

blocks.title: Two money changers
blocks.text: So Rashi explains the difference between a *navon* and a *chacham*. One of the sages of the *Gemara* was asked by a Christian, Arius, what the difference is (the Rebbe has a *sicha* about it), and answered with a *mashal*: two money changers, one rich and one an entrepreneur. When the rich one has no business, he waits. When the go-getter has no business, he goes knocking on doors and gets business.

A *chacham* sits and learns; if a *chiddush* comes, it comes, and if not, there is nothing he can do. When the *navon* gets no *chiddush*, he can go get it, whenever he wants to understand something. That means he reaches up to the *Keser* and brings out the *chachma* at will: the advantage of a *navon*.

phrases.he: (ומכל מקום מה שבהשגה דבינה מבין השגה חדשה מתוך ההשגה זו,
phrases.en: the ability to get a *chiddush* within even the same *hasaga*,
the source of that ability comes from *havein b'chachma*,
because that's already like a thing of understanding one thing from something else,

blocks.text: Another parenthesis. **The ability to get a *chiddush* within even the same *hasaga*** (comprehension), *chachma* of *bina*, is a much lower level; nevertheless **the source of that ability comes from *havein b'chachma*, because that's already like a thing of understanding one thing from something else**, only within the same thing you are learning. It comes from finding the *chachma* and carrying it from one thing to another. The difference: *chachma* of *bina* is in a revealed *sechel*; *bina* of *chachma* is in the hidden source of the *sechel*, in *chachma*.

sections.title: Daas is the bond of feeling, not the learning itself; its length, breadth and depth
sections.summary: What people call *ha'amakas hadaas* is not the delving itself, which is *hisbonenus*; *daas* is binding one's feeling to the concept, the caring that drives the *iyun* deeper. *Daas* too is long or short, broad or narrow, strong or light, and a light *daas*, like a child's, lacks depth and is easily turned to the opposite.

phrases.en: based on what we explained until now,
this that the world calls *ha'amakas hadaas*, deepening your *daas*,
this is not actually the delving into an idea.
like reaching the *omek hamusag* of *bina*.
for this learning process has no connection to *daas*.

blocks.text: **Based on what we explained until now, this that the world calls *ha'amakas hadaas*, deepening your *daas***, is not the learning process: **this is not actually the delving into an idea.** That is *hisbonenus*. It brings you to the *omek hamusag*, the depth of *bina*, up to the depth of *chachma*, brings *chiddushim*, and brings it all back down to *bina*, to being a *mevin* (one who understands). All of that depends on *hisbonenus*, not on *ha'amakas hadaas*.

So it is not going deeper **like reaching the *omek hamusag* of *bina***, from the outside of *bina* to its depth; that is not what *ha'amakas hadaas* means, **for this learning process has no connection to *daas*.** So what is *daas*?

phrases.he: אך הדעת הוא בחינת התקשרות הרגשתו במושג ביותר,
phrases.en: *Daas* means to connect your feeling very deeply to the idea that you understand.

phrases.he: והוא שמביא לידי בחינת העמקה במושג,
phrases.en: this is what causes you to study the idea deeper
after you did the initial *iyun*.

phrases.he: שהוא רק כמו בחינת כלי לעומק ההשגה כנזכר לעיל.
phrases.en: So this *ha'amakas hadaas* is only a tool,

blocks.text: ***Daas* means to connect your feeling very deeply to the idea that you understand**: to feel it is deeply, personally relevant, to associate with it, sympathize with it, to be emotionally sensitive to it, so that you feel it is connected to you.

blocks.title: The chicken story again
blocks.text: As this *HaYom Yom* says, the main thing for understanding *Chassidus* is a *daas* for it: feel it is personally relevant and you will understand even something very hard. Its example is from the *Gemara*: Rabbi Meir (he thinks it was Rabbi Meir) kept bringing genius arguments that a chicken was kosher, and they told him to leave it, it was not kosher. He answered that all these arguments were said to him by a simple peasant woman. Because it was her chicken and it really bothered her, she made arguments of the kind the *Tannaim* and *Amoraim*, far more advanced in Talmudic law, would discuss.
blocks.outOfPlace: The chicken story was first told in class 12, at line 21; here it is retold for its point about daas.

blocks.text: If there's a will, there's a way: if it is really important to you, you will understand. That is why *daas* matters. Not because it makes you understand, but because it makes you care, and if you care you will do the *hisbonenus* automatically, and understand.

This *ha'amakas hadaas*, the personal relevance you feel, **is what causes you to study the idea deeper after you did the initial *iyun*.** Once you have the basics clear, what will make you push your mind further, to *chiddushim* and the depth of *chachma*? You need the motivation.

blocks.title: Passing the test, and free time
blocks.text: In school you do your *iyun*, memorize the material and pass your test; that takes only *iyun*. Making *chiddushim* means you are interested, something you do in your free time because you care. You can't really be made to do that for a test.

**So this *ha'amakas hadaas* is only a tool**: a way to get yourself to use your *bina* to analyze more deeply, which gives the depth of understanding. It does not bring the depth itself; it gets you to study more deeply so you understand more deeply.

blocks.text: Now: *daas* too has depth, length and width. This matters because the depth comes through the length and the width. Someone may say he has no deep *daas* for *Chassidus*: he learned it and knows the basic thing, but does not feel it is personally relevant to him, so what can he do? As study of the length and width of the explanations brings the *omek hamusag*, so working on the length and width of *daas* brings its depth: *ha'amakas hadaas*, which will move you to study more deeply.

***Daas* also has a length, width, and a depth.** **For example, some people have a short *daas*, like a short attention span. and some people have a long attention span**: how long you can sit on the idea. The other length of *daas*, as Reb Hillel explains, is wanting to bring the idea down into many *osios* (letters).

So you want to hear it and talk about it a long time, but also "you'll want to get a t-shirt, and a hat, and a bumper sticker": many *osios*, bringing it down into physical things. **And there are some people that have a broad, a wide *daas*, but it's not long**: it comes out in many things but does not come down far. Without length it stays in the book, an intellectual discussion, never down to physical *osios*.

blocks.title: "That reminds me of golf"
blocks.text: A wide *daas* for a thing talks about it from all angles and brings it up all through the day, connected to all different things. Maybe not long, just discussion. Whatever comes up, "that reminds me of golf." Always golf. Knowing all about it is the *bina*; connecting it to every part of life is a wide *daas*.

A wide *daas* can also hold two opposites at once, see both sides of an argument. A narrow *daas* is interested in politics, say, but only in the Republican side, a narrow aspect. So in *Chassidus*: only *avoda'dike maamarim* (discourses on divine service), or only *haskala'dike maamarim* (discourses of intellectual explanation), only one Rebbe's discourses, or only *maamarim* and not *sichos*, letters or stories. Interest in one aspect alone is a narrow *daas*.

A wide *daas* does not see the two as contradicting; it can hold both because it is interested in something higher, deeper. Length and width come from the depth: the deeper the source, the wider and longer. Someone interested in the real depth of politics, the issues themselves, is interested in both sides.

And so with someone really interested in *Chassidus* itself. **Like somebody who has a strong *daas***: once he connects to something he is totally engrossed and firmly bound to it, hard to move from his opinion or distract, for hours or days or years. Once he has made up his mind, that's it: this is how he sees things and feels things.

**Or a light *daas*, like women**: women are very good at multitasking, usually much better at it than men, because usually their *daas* is lighter; they don't get so engrossed in one thing. Men are usually firmer about their opinion, women more flexible. That is a *daas kal* (a light *daas*).

But a *daas kal* can also mean *temimus'dik* (innocent, wholehearted): it has only one *kav* (measure), as it says a *tam* (a simple, wholehearted person) has one *kav* of *daas*. He can't lie or be sneaky so much: if he should be nice, he is nice. He can't feel he should be nice and at the same time act mean.
It is harder for women to do that, and that is why women are not judges: a judge must put aside the compassion he feels, his *temimus'dike daas*, his one *kav*, and see it from the other side.

You have to hear both sides, feel both and see where each comes from, without getting stuck in either. Multitasking that comes from not connecting too much to any one thing is different from holding a connection to two things at once, which is the width of *daas*. A judge sees it from one point of view, then from the other, and feels no contradiction.

blocks.question: Why don't we speak of strong and light by bina or chachma?
blocks.text: Strong and light here are the equivalent, as he will say, of deep and not so deep. But *daas* is connecting, your mental grasp on a thing, so the expression is strong: a strong connection, a strong feeling. *Bina* and *chachma* are more objective and removed; you would not say you have a strong feeling for them.

**Or a light *daas*, like women** whose *daas* is light. What is a light *daas*? **That means that the *daas* is not so deep. And automatically, if the *daas* isn't so deep, it's also not so long and it's not so wide.**
Men tend to connect much deeper to whatever they're doing and get much more engrossed in it; they become obsessed with it and it takes over their life. Women tend not to do that as much.

He will explain that though *bina* and *daas* are tools that work together, they are opposite: more *daas* at a moment means less *bina*, and the reverse. *Daas* brings more *bina* afterwards, but at the moment a lighter *daas* gives better *bina*. That is why women also have *bina yeseira* (an extra measure of *bina*): it's kind of a trade-off.

**Therefore, it's not so hard to entice the child to the opposite**: to distract him and convince him the other way. **On the other hand, an adult** has a much deeper connection to what he understands or wants, and you can't shake him quickly. If this is his opinion, that's it; if he wants it, he is obsessed with it. **So that's called a deep *daas***, and with it automatically comes a long and wide *daas* in that thing.

Women have more *daas* than a child; a child has no *daas*. Women have a light *daas*, for one *kav* at a time. Men have a strong *daas*: they get much more obsessed with what they get into, but can also hold both sides of a thing at once.

sections.title: Daas focuses, bina spreads out: both together, to the root of chachma and bina
sections.summary: *Iyun* pauses on each point but at once spreads out into a broad picture; *daas* only gathers all the mind onto this one idea, the opposite of spreading. Yet it is *daas*, interest in the right place, that carries the *iyun* to the depths of *chachma* and *bina*: *daas* is hidden in *bina*, and Moshe, who was *daas*, merited the fiftieth gate.

blocks.text: **Which the *iyun* of *bina* itself is really the opposite of this idea of focusing and limiting yourself to just one idea.** *Daas* gets fixated on one idea; *bina* pulls it apart, compares and contrasts its parts, sees how they work together. **Even though when a person is doing *iyun* in *bina*, they dwell on each thing** at first, not moving on until this point is understood, **but immediately it starts to expand**: there's this and there's that, and a third thing and a fourth, and you see how they all fit together.

As here: we dwelt on *bina*, then moved on to *chachma* and dwelt on that, and now on *daas*, and the picture keeps getting bigger. That is the whole point of *bina*: to understand all the points and how they work together.

blocks.title: The watchmaker and the detective
blocks.text: A watchmaker takes a watch apart and looks at each piece carefully under a magnifying glass to see what is broken. He spends a lot of time on each part, but he is after the big picture: how to put it back together and fix it. Or a detective, focusing on each clue to figure out what happened. Yet each needs a very big interest in the details; without it, no time spent on them and no proper analysis.
So *daas* is not a process of thinking. It is not a cognitive process of understanding, not a learning process. It is the focus that motivates you to really learn and do the proper analysis.

blocks.text: **On the other hand, the focus and limiting of *ha'amakas hadaas*** is, on the contrary, gathering all the power of the mind onto this concept alone. **The whole idea of *daas* is only the focus.** It builds no big picture; you are totally engrossed in what you are doing now, and hear and see nothing else.

There are stories of people *davenen* or learning who did not hear or know what was going on around them. It sounds like a level not for a regular person. But really it is very easy for anybody: develop an interest in what you are doing, and automatically you will have a very strong *daas*, a very strong concentration and focus on it.

blocks.title: The kid in front of the video
blocks.text: Stick any kid in front of a TV or a video "and bam, they're out": they don't see you or hear you or know anything. It is just how connected you are. A video makes it easy, with moving pictures, sounds and music. But as you study an idea, do *iyun* in it, you develop an interest; your *daas* connects to it, and you become very engrossed in it and very connected to it.

blocks.text: This focus, totally engrossed in what you are doing now and forgetting everything else, **this is the opposite of the way that *iyun* takes an idea and it tries to spread it out and get a broad picture of the idea.** Learning *halacha*, you want all the laws, everything about *Shabbos*, the whole picture. But right now you are learning one law, and without the *daas* to focus on it alone, you won't analyze it properly. Then you have to move from point to point and step back to see how they fit together.

blocks.text: So you need both, in the right balance: how deep to go, and how much to force yourself on to build the picture. That is why *chazara* (review) is very good: you focus on each thing yet keep going and build the big picture, which also helps you understand; then you come back with everything you learned and go deeper, and again. Learn one thing until you understand it perfectly and you could go forever, because there is always deeper. So the balance of *daas* and *bina*: stop and focus on this until you understand it, and keep moving to build the whole picture.

One more difference. *Daas* does not focus because it wants to understand; it focuses because you like the idea, are connected to it and interested in it. It likes where it is and wants to stay and savor it. *Bina* is after a goal, to understand, so it wants to go on. *Bina* is what makes you understand; but without *daas* you won't use your *bina* enough, and it won't accomplish what it should.

In Yiddish, *der klep mit dem arainleigen zich gor*: **when you grasp an idea and it really settles into you very well.** *Amkus hadaas*, being totally preoccupied with it, is the opposite of the breadth of *bina*. Yet it is what makes you *me'ayen* (analyze) in the right place: **it's this interest that causes your *iyun* to keep going deeper and deeper into the idea, which will bring you eventually to the depth of *chachma* and *bina*.** Without it you understand only the external idea. A deep *daas* is basically knowing what you are after; with your interest in the right place, you understand better.

As it says: one who learns in order to teach is given the means to learn and to teach. You might think that learning is hard enough, and teaching will leave no time to learn. No: you will have time for both. And one who learns in order to do, to live it, is given the means to learn and to teach, to keep and to do.

Why? Because why you learn, where your interest lies, is your *daas*, and the deeper into the essence of the idea you connect it, the more surely your *iyun* goes to the right place and finds the depth. The real depth of the Torah is that it is not just for you: it is for others too, and for action. Learning to bring it to action gets you its essence, and you understand much more quickly, because you are looking in the right place, from the Torah's point of view, and everything fits. Don't go after the *etzem* and you won't get the depth: learn just to know esoteric babble, and "you'll know esoteric babble, that's it."

With this inner interest you get not only the depth of *bina* but *chiddushim*: the more you apply yourself, the more you succeed, and you connect your *koach hamaskil*, your source of new ideas and ingenuity, and bring out new ideas in your understanding.

**And this is what it says that *daas* is hidden in the mouth of the mother.** The *Ima* (mother) is *bina*, understanding. Outwardly *bina* looks like the opposite of *daas*, as if it had not much *daas*. But hidden behind the ability to understand is a very deep interest, a deep *daas*, and that is what gives the understanding.

blocks.text: **Like it says**: Moshe, who is *daas*, merited *bina*. His soul was the level of *daas*, a very deep connection to and interest in everything, **so he merited *bina*, to understand everything**: **which that's the 50th gate of *bina***, the inner depth of *bina* that reaches up to the *Keser*.

**Because the two are interdependent**: they go and come together. *Pirkei Avos* says, "If there is no *daas* there is no *bina*; if there is no *bina* there is no *daas*." **Like it's explained in many places in the *Kesavim***, the Alter Rebbe's long *maamarim*. **And that is enough for a *mevin* to understand.**
